posts.cooked:
I heard that shopify has officially made b2b features for other plans after it was exclusively for shopify plus.

Do you still use apps such as BSS, Sami, clay, massy ..etc. ? or they’re dead ?

Hi @ishaklekbir Welcome To Shopify Community So Yes, that’s correct — as of April 2, 2026, Shopify made key B2B features available on Basic, Grow, and Advanced plans, not just Plus. This includes up to 3 active B2B catalogs, company profiles, payment terms, volume pricing, ACH payments (U.S. only), and vaulted credit cards, all at no additional cost. Unlimited catalogs, direct catalog-to-company assignment, partial payments, and deposits are still Plus-only. shopifyshopify

As for BSS, Sami, Clay, Massy, etc. — they’re not dead, but their role has shifted. Native B2B now covers the basics well enough that a lot of smaller wholesale setups don’t strictly need an app anymore. Apps like BSS still get chosen when a store needs things native B2B doesn’t do, like:

  • More than 3 pricing tiers/catalogs (native is Markets-based and capped at 3)
  • Direct per-company or per-customer (not per-market) pricing
  • More granular approval workflows, custom registration forms, or tiered discount logic beyond simple volume pricing

So it’s less “app vs native” now and more “check if native covers your case first, and only install an app for the specific gap it doesn’t fill.” Hope this helps solve your problem, and if it does, don’t forget to like and mark it as the solution. Thank you!

posts.cooked:
Worth adding a practical way to actually test this rather than guessing: since native B2B now covers volume pricing and company profiles reasonably well, the fastest way to check if you can drop an app like BSS or Clay is to look at your actual pricing structure and count your real tiers. If you’re running 3 or fewer distinct wholesale price levels and pricing is genuinely per-market rather than per-individual-customer, native B2B likely covers your case entirely now, and removing the app just saves the monthly cost with no functional loss.

Where it gets more nuanced: if your current app-based setup uses customer tags or metafields to assign custom pricing per individual account (rather than per market/catalog), that’s the exact gap native B2B still doesn’t close, since native pricing tiers are catalog-based, not account-specific. A lot of older wholesale setups were built exactly this way because it was the only option before B2B existed at all, so it’s worth actually checking how your current app assigns pricing internally before assuming a straightforward “just switch to native” migration, since a like-for-like feature comparison sometimes hides a structural difference in how pricing gets assigned underneath.

One more thing worth flagging for anyone migrating: test the switch on a duplicate/dev theme first if you go this route, since removing a pricing app mid-operation while customers have active carts or saved payment methods tied to the app’s system can cause a rocky transition if done live without a fallback plan.

Best,
Vikash Jha - Apploy

posts.cooked:
Shopify’s native B2B features can be a good fit for stores with relatively straightforward wholesale requirements. However, if you need customer-specific pricing, tiered/volume discounts, flexible wholesale rules, or different pricing setups for different customers, a dedicated wholesale pricing app can still be useful.

One option worth looking at is B2B Guru – Wholesale Pricing. It’s designed to help Shopify merchants manage B2B and retail pricing from the same store, with features such as customer-specific pricing, tiered pricing, flexible discounts, and custom shipping discounts.

So I wouldn’t say wholesale pricing apps are obsolete. For simpler B2B setups, Shopify’s native tools may be enough, while merchants with more customized pricing requirements may still benefit from an app like B2B Guru.

You can take a look at B2B Guru – Wholesale Pricing here: B2B Guru Wholesale Pricing app - Easy B2B Wholesale Pricing Discount, B2B Pricing, B2B ordering | Shopify App Store

posts.cooked:
Good question, and the three answers above cover the pricing side well. One dimension nobody has mentioned: what native B2B covers and what it still does not, once you get past pricing.

Native now handles company profiles, catalogs, volume pricing and payment terms on every paid plan. What it does not do is act on those payment terms. Shopify records that a company is on Net 30 and shows the order as Overdue once the due date passes, but nothing stops that company placing the next order while it owes you. There is no credit limit field anywhere in Shopify. The only native lever is per company, under Customers > Companies > the company > Checkout > Edit > Submit all orders as drafts for review, and it is manual in both directions: someone turns it on when an account goes bad and has to remember to turn it off when they pay.

Reminders are half-covered natively: up to five payment reminder emails, sent on the due date or a set number of days after it, using your own notification template. Nothing before the due date.

So the practical answer to your question depends on which job you are asking about. For pricing, native has genuinely taken over the simple cases, as @VikashJ described. For getting paid, native has not, and that is a different shelf of apps from BSS or Sami.

Disclosure: I build one of those, Credit Guard. It sets a credit limit per company and places a credit hold at checkout when a company is over its limit or has an overdue invoice, with a per-company bypass. It needs companies and payment terms, so it works alongside the native setup rather than replacing a pricing app.

One angle nobody has mentioned yet: the case where distributors need the catalog and their own prices via API, outside your storefront (feeding their own shop or ERP). Native B2B and most pricing apps only apply prices at storefront/checkout level. A pattern that works well is a small middleware in front of the Admin GraphQL API: one scoped API key per partner, pricing rules computed server-side (e.g. % off retail), Shopify stays the system of record, and no partner ever gets an Admin token. Two lessons from running one in production: pin and actively track the Admin API version (we had weight/weightUnit disappear from ProductVariant after a version bump, which broke the catalog endpoint with a generic upstream error), and return money values as strings in JSON. Write-up of the setup, if useful: Aleta B2B API: a Shopify-Backed Catalog for Swiss Distributors · Bulle, Fribourg | d-side (disclosure: I built it).

posts.cooked:
@ishaklekbir Adding one angle the replies haven’t covered yet.

Native covers the simple cases well, as Mustafa_Ali and VikashJ said. When stores still keep or add an app in 2026, it’s usually for one of these:

  1. More than 3 price tiers, or per-account pricing below Plus.
  2. Sales reps ordering for the accounts they manage. Native lets staff place draft orders for company locations from the admin, but there’s no storefront portal where a rep logs in and orders as the customer.
  3. Credit limits on net terms, as sainthesam described.
  4. ERP or accounting sync for price lists and orders.

One more thing to check when you compare apps: several B2B apps cap how many B2B orders each plan includes per month. That’s fine at low volume, but the bill moves with your wholesale growth, so read the plan limits and not just the feature list.

Disclosure: I work on B2Bridge, which covers those four in one app with no monthly B2B order cap. So to answer your question: not dead, but the reasons to install one have narrowed to the gaps above.

Still using them — but for a narrower slice than in 2025, and the deciding question is how much pricing structure you actually need.

The replies above cover the native side well: if you run three price levels or fewer and can organize buyers into companies and catalogs, native B2B does that on every paid plan now.

The slice where a lightweight app still makes sense is the opposite shape: you don’t want to restructure anything into catalogs — you just want one flat wholesale percentage for a defined group, applied automatically at checkout. No codes to send, no price lists to maintain. Two eligibility shapes cover most cases: a customer tag (wholesale customers you approve one by one), or the B2B company itself — buyers checking out in their company context get the discount on each line item.

We built Wholesale Price Manager for exactly that middle case: one percentage rule, eligibility by customer tag or by B2B company, applied automatically at checkout. Deliberately narrow — no tiered pricing, no multiple price lists, no minimum orders. If you need those, native catalogs or a fuller wholesale suite is the better fit.

What’s your actual structure — a flat wholesale percentage for a group, or per-account tiers? That decides native versus app more than anything else.

Short answer: it depends on how many price levels you really have.

Native B2B on Basic, Grow and Advanced gives you 3 active catalogs, shared across all your B2B markets, and catalogs attach to markets, not to companies. So:

  • 1 to 3 price levels, same for every buyer in a market: native catalogs are enough. Don’t add an app.
  • 4+ levels, or one big account that negotiated its own prices: you hit the limit. Your options are Plus (direct catalog assignment to companies), or an app that prices on top of Companies.

If you go the app route, check two things: does it read native Companies and locations (not just customer tags), and can you see what a given buyer will pay before they order.

Disclosure: I built Pactly, which adds price tiers on top of native Companies for non-Plus stores. Happy to answer questions either way.
